title: What Are the Sacraments? Baptism and the Lord's Supper
subtitle: The two signs Christ commanded His church to keep. Who baptism is for, what happens at the Table, and why churches that share one Lord have never shared one answer.
triageNote: That Christ commanded both signs, that He gave His church baptism and the Table and meant them to be kept until He comes, and that in them grace is God's act before it is ever our response, sits near the center of the faith. A church that abandons them has abandoned something Christ Himself instituted. But who should be baptized, by what mode, and what exactly happens when the bread is broken, those questions have divided faithful churches for five centuries, and divided them among people who love the same Lord and open the same book. Keep the signs with your whole weight. Hold your account of their inner workings with humility. The command is far plainer than the mechanism.
question:
On the night He was betrayed, Jesus took bread. Before He ascended, He commanded His church to make disciples and baptize them. Two acts, water and bread and wine, and there is no Christian tradition on earth that does not practice them in some form. The questions this page takes up are the two the church has never stopped arguing. Who is baptism for, the person who professes faith, or also the children of those who do? And what happens at the Table, is Christ present in the bread, with it, through it, or remembered by it? Even the name is contested. Sacrament comes from sacramentum, the Latin word for a soldier's oath of allegiance, the word the old Latin Bible chose to render the Greek mysterion. Ordinance is the word many Baptists prefer, an act ordained by Christ, chosen partly to guard against the idea that the rite works on its own. The word you reach for already leans toward an answer, which is a warning about how deep the disagreement runs.

The practices themselves are as old as anything we can see. The Didache, a church manual usually dated somewhere between roughly AD 50 and 120, gives instructions for baptizing in running water, allows pouring water on the head three times if no living water can be found, and restricts the Eucharist to the baptized. Justin Martyr, writing his First Apology in Rome around 155, describes the baptism of those who are persuaded and believe, and says of the bread and cup that we do not receive these as common bread and common drink. Both signs, then, from the church's first generations, and already carrying more weight than mere custom. But the early evidence does not settle the later disputes. The Didache never tells us whether the households being baptized included infants. Justin's reverence does not come with a metaphysics attached. The controversies came later, and when they came, they came hard.

The hardest of them can be dated. In October 1529, at Philip of Hesse's castle in Marburg, Martin Luther and Huldrych Zwingli met to unite the Reformation. They agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles, on Scripture, on the Trinity, on justification by faith, on nearly everything two reformers could be asked. The fifteenth article was the Supper. The story has come down that Luther wrote hoc est corpus meum, this is my body, in chalk on the table in front of him and would not move from it. Zwingli held that is meant signifies, as it plainly does when Jesus says I am the door. Witnesses report that Luther told the Swiss they had a different spirit. The colloquy failed, the Reformation divided at its own family meal, and the division has never healed. This page walks through what each tradition actually claims, at its strongest, and asks how a church is supposed to hold two signs its Lord commanded when His people cannot agree on what they are.
whyItMatters:
Start in the pastor's study, because that is where this doctrine stops being abstract. A young couple sits down with a newborn and asks whether she should be baptized. Whatever the pastor answers, he is not reciting a preference. He is telling them what that child is to the church of God, whether the promise Peter preached at Pentecost has her name inside it already or waits for her own lips to claim it, whether the water says God has acted or says she has answered. Two godly traditions give two opposite answers to that couple, and both do it from Scripture. The question follows the child her whole life. What was done to me in that font, or not done? Was it grace, or was it only water too early?

Then stand at the Table, because that is where the stakes rise highest. Every week, somewhere in every tradition, a Christian takes bread and hears the words this is my body. What is in his hands? The Catholic answers, the body of Christ, truly, substantially. The Lutheran answers, the body of Christ, in and with and under the bread. The Reformed believer answers, bread, and yet by the Spirit a true feeding on the true Christ. The memorialist answers, bread, carrying the weight a wedding ring carries, which is not nothing. These are not four moods. They are four accounts of how the grace of God actually reaches a human being, whether it comes through creatures He appoints or immediately to faith alone, and behind them stand different readings of the Incarnation itself, of what Christ's ascended body is and where it can be. Tell me what you believe happens at the Table and I can tell you a great deal about what you believe happens everywhere else.

And there is a wound in this doctrine that ought to be named at the start. The Supper is the meal of unity. One bread, one body, Paul says. Yet no Christian practice makes our division more visible. A Catholic and a Baptist can pray together, grieve together, evangelize together, and cannot commune together. Marburg was not the exception; it became the rule. Whole traditions fence their tables against members of other traditions who confess the same creed. Perhaps that is faithfulness, each side guarding what it believes the sign to be. Perhaps it is scandal. Probably it is both at once, which is why this page ends where it does, with the argument fully honored and the grief fully felt. The signs were given to bind the church to her Lord and to itself. We have kept the first binding better than the second.

positions.name: Believer's baptism (credobaptism)
positions.inOneLine: Baptism is for disciples. The New Testament pattern is faith first, then water, and the new covenant community is defined by new birth, not by birth.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin where every baptism in the New Testament begins, with a person who believes. Repent and be baptized, Peter preaches at Pentecost, and those who received his word were baptized. The Ethiopian eunuch hears the good news about Jesus from Philip and says, see, here is water, what prevents me from being baptized, and the answer is nothing, because he believes. Lydia, the jailer, Crispus, Saul of Tarsus himself. Read the book of Acts from end to end and you will not find a single baptism narrated apart from faith. The Great Commission carries the same order. Make disciples of all nations, baptizing them, teaching them. The them who are baptized are the disciples who have been made. I do not claim the narrative settles everything by itself. I claim that when the New Testament shows us baptism, this is the only thing it ever shows, and a practice with no example and no command in the whole apostolic record should carry the burden of proof, not hold the ancient ground.

But my case does not finally rest on counting narratives. It rests on what the new covenant is. Jeremiah promised a covenant not like the covenant God made with the fathers, and he named the difference. They shall all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest. The covenant with Abraham embraced a household and a nation, believers and unbelievers together, and so its sign rightly went to infants who might or might not ever trust the God of their fathers. The new covenant has no such mixed membership. Its members are those who know the Lord, every one of them, forgiven, regenerate, written on the heart. That is why the sign changed and why its subjects changed with it. Baptism does not mark descent from believing parents. It marks union with a crucified and risen Christ, buried with Him by baptism into death, raised to walk in newness of life, and Peter dares to call it an appeal to God for a good conscience. An infant can be loved, blessed, prayed over, and raised in the discipline and instruction of the Lord, and in my church she is. What she cannot do is appeal, and I will not put on her body a sign whose meaning the Bible states in the vocabulary of faith.

The early evidence, honestly handled, does not embarrass me. The Didache assumes instruction and fasting before baptism. Justin Martyr around 155 describes the baptism of those who are persuaded and believe that what we teach is true. Around the year 200 Tertullian, our first writer to discuss the baptism of little children directly, counsels delay, let them come when they are able to know Christ. I will be honest in the other direction too, because my view requires it of me. By the middle of the third century infant baptism is plainly established. Origen calls it a tradition from the apostles, and Cyprian's council debated only whether to wait until the eighth day. I do not think third-century practice outweighs first-century pattern, and I notice the same centuries drifting on other matters. But I concede that if infant baptism were an innovation, I would expect some record of the controversy its arrival caused, and there is none. That silence is the paedobaptist's best historical card, and I do not pretend it is a low one.

Where am I pressed hardest by Scripture itself? Two places, and I will name them plainly. The household baptisms, Lydia's house, the jailer's house, the house of Stephanas, where the apostles baptized families the way Abraham circumcised one, and no ages are given. I answer that the same narratives extend faith to the household where they extend baptism, the jailer's whole house heard the word and rejoiced that he had believed, but I grant that I am reading silence, and so is my opponent. And Acts 2:39, the promise is for you and for your children, a Jewish preacher speaking covenant language to Jewish ears. I answer with the rest of Peter's own sentence, and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to Himself, which makes the promise reach as wide as the calling, not as wide as the bloodline. But I feel the weight of two thousand years of children carrying the covenant sign, and of parents who long to mark their child as God's. I tell those parents that their child is holy to the Lord in Paul's sense, welcomed, prayed for, raised inside the promise. I only insist that the water wait for the faith it was given to confess.
advocates: Thomas R. Schreiner and Shawn D. Wright (Believer's Baptism)
Paul K. Jewett (Infant Baptism and the Covenant of Grace)
the Baptist, Anabaptist, and free-church traditions broadly

positions.name: Infant baptism (paedobaptism, covenantal)
positions.inOneLine: The children of believers belong to the covenant community and receive its sign, as they have since Abraham. God's promise runs to households, and grace speaks before the child can answer.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin two thousand years before the New Testament, because that is where the argument actually begins. When God cut His covenant with Abraham, He said, I will establish My covenant between Me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations, to be God to you and to your offspring after you. And He commanded the sign of that covenant, circumcision, to be given to infants on the eighth day. For twenty centuries, the children of believers carried the sign of the covenant of grace before they could speak. That is not background. That is the world every apostle lived in, the assumption in every Jewish bone at Pentecost. So when Peter stands up and cries, repent and be baptized, and then immediately adds, for the promise is for you and for your children, no hearer in Jerusalem could have taken that as a revocation of their children's place. It is Genesis 17 preached in Acts 2. If God had ended the membership of believers' children in His covenant people, after two millennia, we would expect a word of explanation, an argument, a controversy like the one circumcision itself caused at Jerusalem. There is none. The burden of proof does not sit where my Baptist brother puts it. Silence about infant baptism is exactly what you would expect if nothing had changed.

And the New Testament does more than stay silent. Paul explicitly joins the two signs. In him you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, buried with Him in baptism. Baptism is the circumcision of the new covenant, the sign of the same covenant of grace in its fuller administration. The apostles baptized the way Abraham circumcised, by households. Lydia was baptized, and her household. The jailer was baptized at once, he and all his family. Paul baptized the household of Stephanas. Three households in a handful of narrated baptisms, and the pattern is so unremarkable to the writers that no one pauses to explain it. Add the Lord Himself, indignant when the disciples turned the children away. Let the little children come to Me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven. I do not build the doctrine on that verse alone. I ask why the church that follows this Lord would give His covenant children less standing than Israel's children had.

Understand what I am claiming and what I am not. I do not teach that the water regenerates the child by its own working, and the Reformed confessions I stand in explicitly deny it. Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, God's own promise made visible on a particular body, to be answered by faith when God grants it, what our fathers called improving one's baptism across a whole life. And here is the deepest beauty of it, the thing I most want my credobaptist brother to see. Infant baptism gets the direction of grace right. The child contributes nothing, decides nothing, achieves nothing. She is loved first, claimed first, spoken to first, and spends her life answering. That is not a distortion of the gospel. That is the gospel, grace preceding faith the way it precedes it in every conversion, drawn on a baby in water. When believers' baptism is made the only baptism, the sign risks turning around to face the other way, becoming chiefly my testimony, my decision, my act of obedience, and the church quietly relocates the center of gravity from God's promise to my profession.

Where am I pressed hardest? I will say it without flinching. No verse in the New Testament describes the baptism of an infant, and I believe none does, so my case is built from covenant theology, household texts, and the absence of a revocation, an argument from the architecture of Scripture rather than from an explicit command. Jeremiah's new covenant, where all shall know the Lord, is the strongest text against me, and the credobaptist reading of it is serious. I answer that Jeremiah preaches the covenant's consummation, and that Peter still says the promise is for your children on the very day that covenant is poured out, and that even now the visible church baptizes some, on any view, who prove not to know the Lord. But I concede the not like the covenant I made with their fathers is a sword my opponent wields with real skill. And I carry a pastoral wound of my own, the millions baptized in infancy who were never discipled, for whom the sign became an inoculation instead of a summons. That is not the doctrine's fault. It is the church's, and mine. But my brother is right that my practice has more room for that corruption than his, and honesty requires me to say so.
advocates: Sinclair Ferguson and the Reformed and Presbyterian tradition broadly

positions.name: Transubstantiation (the Roman Catholic view)
positions.inOneLine: At the consecration the bread and wine become, in their whole substance, the body and blood of Christ, while the appearances of bread and wine remain. He said this is My body, and the church has never dared to correct Him.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin with the words themselves, because everything I hold follows from taking them at their word. On the night He was betrayed, the Lord took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said, this is My body, which is given for you. He did not say, this represents My body, or this will help you remember My body. Language was not poor that night. The Word made flesh, who chose every word, said is. And He had prepared His disciples for it in the hardest sermon He ever preached. Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life in you, He said at Capernaum, and when the crowd recoiled, this is a hard saying, who can listen to it, He did not soften it into metaphor. He sharpened it, My flesh is true food and My blood is true drink, and He let them walk away. Teachers correct misunderstandings. Jesus watched disciples abandon Him over the literal sense and never once called them back to explain that He had only been speaking figuratively. I ask you to sit with that scene before you dismiss my view as medieval.

And the apostolic church heard Him exactly this way. Paul warns the Corinthians that whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord, and that some among them are weak and ill, and some have died, for eating without discerning the body. You do not die for mishandling a symbol. The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? Around the year 110, Ignatius of Antioch, a bishop taught within living memory of the apostles, wrote against the docetists that they abstain from the Eucharist because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ. Around 155 Justin Martyr told the Roman emperor that we do not receive these as common bread and common drink, but as the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh. From there the testimony runs unbroken through Irenaeus, Cyril of Jerusalem, Ambrose, Chrysostom. The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 gave the mystery its technical name, transubstantiated, and the Council of Trent in 1551 defined it against the Reformers, but the councils were fencing an ancient treasure, not minting a new one. The church adored what lay on her altars long before she had Aristotle's vocabulary for it.

About that vocabulary, let me say what is often misheard. Transubstantiation is not a claim that we have explained the miracle. It is a claim about what changes and what does not. The substance, the deepest reality of the thing, what it is, becomes wholly the body and blood of Christ. The accidents, everything available to the senses and to science, taste, weight, chemistry, remain the accidents of bread and wine. Thomas Aquinas built the account with borrowed philosophical tools, but the tools serve the mystery, they do not master it, and Thomas himself wrote hymns confessing that sight, touch, and taste are all deceived here, and faith alone suffices. Strip away the terminology and the claim is simple and staggering. The Lord who turned water to wine and multiplied loaves gives His people, until He comes, not a picture of Himself but Himself. Grace does not merely accompany the sacrament. God acts through the creatures He appoints, as He acted through the flesh of the Incarnation itself. A purely symbolic Supper fits a purely spiritual religion. It fits poorly with a faith whose center is the Word become flesh.

Where am I pressed hardest? Scripture says Christ ascended, that heaven must receive Him until the time for restoring all things, and my opponents ask how a true human body can be on ten thousand altars at once. I answer that His presence in the sacrament is sacramental, not local in the ordinary sense, His body present after the manner of substance, not stretched like a thing among things, but I grant the account strains the mind, and Thomas granted it too. I am pressed by Augustine, who could call the sacrament a sign and a figure, language my Protestant brothers quote against me, though I read him confessing sign and reality together rather than sign instead of reality. And I am pressed by the plain grammar of do this in remembrance of Me, which sounds, on its face, closer to Zwingli than to Trent. I answer that a memorial and a presence are not rivals, the Passover was a memorial in which every generation was to see itself brought out of Egypt, and the Mass is remembrance precisely because the One remembered is there. But I know the weight my view must carry, an entire metaphysics resting on one short sentence at a supper table. I carry it because I believe He meant it.
advocates: the Catechism of the Catholic Church

positions.name: Sacramental union (the Lutheran view)
positions.inOneLine: The true body and blood of Christ are present in, with, and under the bread and wine, and are received by the mouth by all who eat, believer and unbeliever alike. The words this is My body require no philosophy and permit no metaphor.
positions.bestCase:
I begin at the same table the Catholic begins at, with the same four words, and I refuse to move from them for anyone. At Marburg in 1529, so the story has come down, Luther chalked hoc est corpus meum on the table and kept returning to it against every argument the Swiss could mount, and I stand with him. This is My body. Christ said it. I did not, and it is not mine to improve. When Zwingli urged that is means signifies, as in I am the door, Luther's answer was that you may read a figure where the text and its setting give you one, a door with hinges is not in the room, but here a man holds bread at a covenant meal on the night of His death and says, this is My body, given for you, and then Paul, decades later, writes that unworthy eating makes a person guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord. Guilty of a body that is absent? Judged for misusing a symbol? The apostle's warning only carries its terror if the thing profaned is actually there. So I confess with the Augsburg Confession of 1530 that the body and blood of Christ are truly present and are distributed to those who eat the Lord's Supper.

But mark where I part from Rome, because my view is not a softened transubstantiation. I refuse the explanation, not the presence. Scripture nowhere says the bread ceases to be bread, and Paul, after the consecration language, still calls it bread three times. The bread remains bread, and it is the body of Christ, both at once, in, with, and under, a sacramental union I do not explain any more than I explain how the divine and human natures are one Christ, which is exactly the analogy the fathers reached for, iron in the fire, fire and iron both fully there. Rome, to my mind, answered a mystery with a theory and then built practices on the theory, adoration of the reserved host, the sacrifice of the Mass, that Scripture never builds. I also refuse Geneva's ladder. The Reformed tell me the Spirit lifts my heart to feed on Christ in heaven. But Christ did not say, ascend to Me. He said, take, eat. The direction of the sacrament is the direction of the whole gospel, God coming down to sinners, grace put into hands and mouths. And His ascended humanity is no prisoner of a location, for the right hand of God is not a chair somewhere in the sky, it is His almighty power everywhere present, and the Christ who fills all things can give His true body where He has promised to give it, in the bread, for you.

For you, those are the words I would die for. Here is the pastoral heart of my whole position. If Christ's presence in the Supper depends on the quality of my faith, on my successful spiritual ascent, then in the hour my faith is weakest, the sacrament is emptiest, and the gift fails exactly when I need it most. But if the body of Christ is objectively there in the bread, given by promise, then the sacrament does not rest on me at all. The weakest believer, the doubting one, the one who cannot feel anything, receives the same Christ as the strongest saint, because the gift was never measured by the receiver. That is why we Lutherans insist, strange as it sounds, that even the unworthy eat the true body, to their judgment rather than their blessing, for that is what Paul says happened at Corinth. The objectivity is the comfort. A sacrament that is only as real as my faith is a mirror. A sacrament that is real before my faith is a gospel.

Where am I pressed hardest? By Chalcedon, and I will not pretend otherwise. The Reformed charge that my doctrine of Christ's ubiquity, His human nature sharing the omnipresence of His divine person, confuses the two natures and edges toward Eutyches, giving me a body that is no longer a human body at all. I answer with the communication of attributes, the person of Christ is one, and what He is and has, He is and has as one undivided person, so the man Jesus is wherever the Son of God is. But I concede this is the deepest water in my system, and that heaven must receive Him until the time for restoring all things reads more naturally on their side than on mine. I hold my ground anyway, for a simple reason. Between a Christology I cannot fully diagram and a promise I would have to reinterpret, I will keep the promise. He said, this is My body. I would rather be found too literal at that table than too clever.

positions.name: Spiritual presence (the Reformed view)
positions.inOneLine: Christ is truly given and truly received at the Table, not by His body descending into the bread, but by the Holy Spirit lifting believers to feed on the whole Christ, ascended in heaven, through faith.
positions.bestCase:
I stand between Wittenberg and Zurich, and I want you to hear from the start that mine is not a compromise position, splitting a difference to keep peace. It is a conviction with its own spine, and Calvin argued it with more heat than he argued almost anything. Against the bare memorialist I insist, the Supper is not chiefly something we do. It is something we are given. The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Participation, koinonia, communion, that is stronger language than remembering. Calvin said the signs are not empty pictures but instruments by which God truly performs what He promises, and that in the Supper believers are given the true body and blood of Christ, so really that the soul is fed on Christ as truly as bread feeds the body. Whatever else you take from my account, take this. Something is given at that Table, and the giver is God.

Against Rome and against my dear, stubborn brother Luther, I insist on something equally biblical, the body of Christ is a true human body, and it has a location. This is not rationalism. It is Christology, the doctrine of the two natures held without confusion, as Chalcedon confessed in 451. The Son of God took a real human nature, and a real human nature is finite, embodied, somewhere. That body rose, and ascended, and Peter preaches that heaven must receive Him until the time for restoring all things. The angels said He would return the way He went. To make His body ubiquitous, present in every loaf on every altar, is, however piously meant, to let the divine nature swallow the human one, and then the very thing that makes the Incarnation our salvation, that He is bone of our bone forever, begins to dissolve. Luther keeps the presence by bending the body. Rome keeps the presence by multiplying the miracle. I will do neither, because I do not have to.

For here is the heart of my account, the piece both sides underestimate. The Holy Spirit. The distance between my table and Christ's ascended body is real, and the Spirit overcomes it, not by dragging Christ down into bread, but by lifting believers up to Him. This is why the oldest line in the church's liturgy, centuries older than these debates, is sursum corda, lift up your hearts, and the people answer, we lift them up to the Lord. The Spirit who unites a believer to Christ in the first place, so that Paul can say we are members of His body, is not defeated by geography. In the Supper that same Spirit makes the sign and the thing signified arrive together for faith, bread in the hand, Christ to the soul, truly, substantially even, Calvin dared to say, but by the Spirit's secret working rather than by a change in the elements or a relocation of the body. Do I understand the mechanism? No, and I refuse to manufacture one. Calvin wrote that this mystery is too lofty for his mind to comprehend or his words to declare, and then said the sentence I have come to love most in this whole literature, I rather experience it than understand it. That is not evasion. That is a man refusing to shrink a gift to the size of his explanation.

Where am I pressed hardest? From both sides at once, which is the price of standing where I stand. Luther's heirs ask me, with an edge, what your Spirit-lifted feeding actually adds to devout remembering, whether spiritual presence is anything more than memorialism with better music, and whether locating the gift in the believer's Spirit-wrought ascent quietly makes my faith the hinge after all. I answer that the feeding is objective on God's side, offered truly in the sign whether or not I rise to it, and that faith receives the gift rather than creating it. But I confess the line is fine, and that in the pews of my own tradition it has often blurred into mere memorial in practice, which suggests the distinction needs more guarding than I would like. And the plain words press me too. This is My body is simply an easier sentence for Wittenberg and Rome than for me, and I know it. I read it as sacramental speech, the sign named by the thing it conveys, as the rock was Christ and the cup is the new covenant. I believe that reading is right. I also believe I should hold it with the humility of a man who is telling the Lord's own grammar what it must mean.
advocates: Robert Letham and the Reformed tradition broadly

positions.name: Memorialism (the Zwinglian and free-church view)
positions.inOneLine: The Supper is a covenant meal of remembrance, proclamation, and pledged allegiance. Christ is present as He is always present with His gathered people. The bread does not contain Him. It announces Him.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin with the words everyone else's account has to work around, because they are the Lord's own statement of purpose. Do this in remembrance of Me. Not, do this to receive My substance. Not, do this and I will descend into it. In remembrance. And Paul, handing on what he received from the Lord Himself, adds the second purpose, for as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes. Remembrance and proclamation, the meal facing backward to a finished cross and forward to a returning King. I did not choose those two words. The text did. And I notice that the only explicit judgment-language in the chapter turns not on failing to detect a substance in the bread but on the Corinthians' contempt for one another at the meal, the rich humiliating the poor, so that discerning the body may well mean discerning the congregation, the body of Christ that Paul has been talking about for two chapters. The Supper's realism, in 1 Corinthians, is horizontal before it is metaphysical.

As for this is My body, Zwingli's point at Marburg in 1529 was not a trick of grammar. It was an observation about how the Bible talks. I am the door. I am the true vine. The seed is the word. The rock was Christ, Paul says of Israel's wilderness, and no one has ever hunted for a mechanism of rock-presence. Scripture's covenant meals speak this way natively. Of the Passover lamb Israel said, in effect, this is the Lord's Passover, it is the sacrifice of the Lord's Passover, and every Jewish household understood that the lamb on their table participated in the meaning of the Exodus without anyone teaching a change of substance. Jesus instituted His Supper inside that very meal, with that very grammar in the room. And when the crowd at Capernaum took His eating language with crude literalism, He Himself said the sentence I would put over this whole debate, it is the Spirit who gives life, the flesh is no help at all, the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. Add Hebrews, where by a single offering He has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified, a sacrifice finished, unrepeatable, needing no re-presentation on any altar, and the shape of my position is complete. The Supper is a sign, and the history of religion teaches what happens when signs are fed, they grow into objects of superstition, and the church ends up adoring bread. The Reformation was fought, in part, to turn our eyes from the elements back to the Christ they point to, who is received by faith alone.

Now let me clear away the sneer that hides inside the word mere, because mere memorialism is a phrase my opponents coined and I decline to wear. A memorial, in Scripture, is not a lesser thing. The Passover was a memorial, and at that table every generation of Israel was commanded to see itself brought out of Egypt, the past made present to faith. A wedding ring is a symbol, and a man does not shrug when his wife removes it. Zwingli's own favorite frame was the sacramentum, the soldier's oath, the public pledge by which a man binds himself to his commander before witnesses. At the Table I remember the covenant, I proclaim the death, and I re-enlist, body and soul, in front of the church, and the church does it together, one loaf, one body. And Christ is present, hear me, I have never once believed in an absent Christ. Where two or three are gathered in My name, there am I among them, He said, and He is, at the Supper as at the sermon and the prayers. What I deny is not the presence of Christ. It is the localizing of that presence in bread, as if the Lord of glory were more in the tray than in His gathered, praying, remembering people.

Where am I pressed hardest? By Paul, mostly, and I will not hide it. Is it not a participation in the blood of Christ, he asks, and koinonia is a thick word, thicker than my account finds comfortable, and the warning that unworthy eaters are guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord, with sickness and death at Corinth behind it, reads more heavily than any symbol-misuse I can point to elsewhere. I answer that covenant signs carry covenant sanctions, that despising the pledge despises the one pledged to, but I grant the Reformed reading of those verses is strong, perhaps the strongest single argument on this whole page. And the early church is not my friend. Ignatius around 110 and Justin around 155 already speak of the Eucharist with a realism beyond my categories, and I must argue that devotion outran doctrine very early, which is possible, the church drifted early on other matters too, but it is a harder brief than inheriting the fathers. I hold my ground because I believe the New Testament itself, read on its own terms, gives me remembrance, proclamation, and communion of the gathered body, and nowhere clearly gives me more. But among the four accounts of the Supper, I may be the one most obligated to admit that many of my own congregations have made the Supper less than even I believe it to be, rushed, occasional, an appendix to the sermon. If my view is right, the meal deserves far more weight than my tradition has often given it, and that failure is ours, not the doctrine's.
advocates: much of the Baptist tradition and modern evangelicalism
many contemporary Baptist and non-denominational statements of faith

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, the charter for baptism itself
biblicalEvidence.summary: Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. Baptism is not a custom the church developed. It is a command the risen Christ issued, bound to discipleship and to the triune name.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It presses any church that treats baptism as optional or incidental. Between the baptism views, each side claims the verse's order.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The credobaptist reads the sequence as decisive, disciples are made, then baptized, then taught, so the baptized are disciples by definition. The paedobaptist answers that the command addresses the mission to the nations, not the age of subjects, that the participles do not fix a chronology, and that when the nations come in, they come in as they always have, households and all. Both agree the verse binds baptism to the church's whole teaching life rather than making it a momentary rite.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Contested, claimed in full by both baptism views
biblicalEvidence.summary: Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to Himself. The first Christian sermon ends with both the call to repentance and the covenant formula about children, side by side in one breath.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It presses both views, which is why both preach it. The credobaptist must handle for your children. The paedobaptist must handle repent and be baptized.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The credobaptist reads the verse whole, the promise extends to the children and to those far off in exactly the same way, as many as the Lord our God calls, so the promise reaches as far as effectual calling, not as far as descent, and the command remains repent first. The paedobaptist hears Peter, a Jew addressing Jews on the day the new covenant is poured out, deliberately echoing Genesis 17, you and your offspring, and argues that no hearer formed by twenty centuries of covenant households could have heard those words as excluding their children until adulthood.

biblicalEvidence.summary: In Him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, having been buried with Him in baptism, in which you were also raised with Him through faith in the powerful working of God. Paul sets circumcision and baptism in direct relation, the strongest single link in the covenantal case that baptism now stands where circumcision stood.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for believer's baptism, which must explain the connection without conceding that baptism inherits circumcision's infant subjects.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The credobaptist points out that the circumcision in view is made without hands, the circumcision of the heart, not the eighth-day rite, and that the verse itself says raised with Him through faith, tying baptism to faith inside the very sentence. So the parallel proves that baptism signifies inward renewal, which is exactly why it belongs to those who believe. The paedobaptist replies that physical circumcision also signified heart-realities, Deuteronomy and Romans say so plainly, and was still commanded for infants, so the argument that a faith-signifying sign cannot go to children proves too much, it would have unmade circumcision itself.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Lydia was baptized, and her household as well. The Philippian jailer was told, believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household, and he was baptized at once, he and all his family. Paul baptized the household of Stephanas. The apostles are shown baptizing by households, the ancient covenant unit.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for believer's baptism, which must account for a repeated household pattern in a book with only a handful of narrated baptisms.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The credobaptist notes that the same narratives extend the word and the joy to the household, the jailer's whole house heard the word of the Lord and rejoiced along with him that he had believed in God, and Stephanas's household appears later devoting themselves to ministry, so every member the text describes is a believer, and no text mentions an infant. Both sides are reading silence, and the credobaptist argues the silence should be read by the explicit pattern of faith-then-baptism everywhere else. The paedobaptist answers that the household formula itself, not the unstated ages, is the point, God still deals with houses, as He did with Abraham's.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? We were buried therefore with Him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. And the Ethiopian eunuch, hearing the gospel, asks, see, here is water, what prevents me from being baptized? Baptism is described in the vocabulary of union with Christ, and narrated as the answer of faith.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for infant baptism, since Paul predicates death, burial, and resurrection life of all the baptized, realities an infant cannot yet be said to have entered by faith.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The paedobaptist replies that Paul writes to a first-generation missionary church, where all the baptized were of course converts, and that circumcision too signified faith-realities, Paul calls it a seal of the righteousness that Abraham had by faith, yet God commanded it for eight-day-old boys, so a sign may speak of faith and still be placed on a child in promise of it. On mode, the paedobaptist adds that burial imagery is one of several baptismal images, alongside washing, clothing, and sprinkling, and notes the Didache already permitted pouring. The credobaptist responds that a promissory sign placed before faith is precisely what Jeremiah said the new covenant would no longer need.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Contested among all four views of the Supper, the words at the center of Marburg
biblicalEvidence.summary: Take, eat, this is My body. And He took a cup, and when He had given thanks He gave it to them, saying, drink of it, all of you, for this is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. Luke adds, do this in remembrance of Me. Four traditions, one sentence, and the Reformation divided over the verb.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It presses every view. The realist traditions must sit with in remembrance of Me. The memorialist must sit with is.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Catholic reads is with full literal force, the substance changed, and remembrance as the mode of a presence, not its substitute. The Lutheran reads is literally but refuses the theory of change, body and bread together, in, with, and under. The Reformed reads it as sacramental speech, the sign named by the gift it truly conveys, so that the words are neither bare metaphor nor local presence. The memorialist reads it alongside I am the door and the rock was Christ, covenant-meal grammar Israel had used at every Passover, with the Lord's own stated purpose, remembrance and proclamation, governing the whole.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The real-presence traditions, with the memorialist's strongest counter-verse inside the same chapter
biblicalEvidence.summary: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life in you. My flesh is true food, and My blood is true drink. The crowd recoils and disciples leave, and Jesus does not soften the words. Ten verses later He says, it is the Spirit who gives life, the flesh is no help at all, the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. The chapter arms both sides.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Verses 53 to 58 are hardest for memorialism. Verse 63 is hardest for every realist reading, and the Reformed claim it as their own.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Catholic and Lutheran read the discourse as eucharistic, the scandal of the leaving disciples proving Jesus meant more than metaphor, and read verse 63 as contrasting Spirit-wrought faith with carnal misunderstanding, not retracting the feeding. The Reformed reads the chapter as teaching a true feeding on Christ by faith, which the Supper later signs and seals, with verse 63 fixing the manner, spiritual, by the Spirit. The memorialist reads the whole discourse as about believing, whoever believes has eternal life stands at its head, so the eating is a vivid figure for faith, and verse 63 is the Lord's own commentary.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Real participation, claimed most strongly by the Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed views
biblicalEvidence.summary: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Then, as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes, and whoever eats and drinks in an unworthy manner is guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord, and for this reason some at Corinth were weak and ill, and some had died.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hardest for memorialism, which must give full weight to participation and to a warning enforced with sickness and death. The proclamation and remembrance language presses back toward the memorial pole.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The realist traditions read koinonia as actual communion in the body and blood, and the Corinthian judgments as the seriousness of profaning a real presence, with the Lutheran adding that the unworthy must therefore truly receive it. The Reformed agrees the participation is real but locates it in the Spirit's uniting work, not in the elements as such. The memorialist reads koinonia as covenant fellowship, the sharers in the one loaf are one body, notes that the Corinthian sin Paul actually names is contempt for the poor at the meal, and takes discerning the body as discerning the congregation, so the sanctions guard the covenant community, not a substance.

weighing:
My judgment, offered as one pastor thinking out loud, not as a verdict you must accept. And you should know from the first sentence where I stand and what I have to gain. I am a Baptist pastor. I baptize believers on profession of faith, and once a month I hold up bread in front of a congregation and say, this is my body, over elements I believe remain bread. I am not a neutral judge of this question. I am a man giving an account of his own practice, and you should weigh what follows accordingly.

On baptism, I am a convinced credobaptist, and the conviction has not weakened with years of testing it. The New Testament shows me faith and water together every single time it shows me anything, and Jeremiah's promise, they shall all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest, still reads to me like the charter of a covenant community entered by new birth rather than by birth. When I stand waist-deep in the water with a person who has come to trust Christ, and I ask them who Jesus is, and they answer in front of the church with their own voice, I believe I am watching baptism do exactly what it was given to do. But I want to name, with its full weight, the objection I have not fully answered, because it deserves better than the quick dismissals it gets in Baptist pulpits, including at times my own. For two thousand years, God gave the children of His people a covenant sign in their infancy. Peter, on the day the new covenant was publicly poured out, said the promise is for you and for your children. The apostles baptized households, and when infant baptism becomes clearly visible in the record, in Origen and Cyprian in the third century, no one anywhere is recorded objecting to it as a novelty. If the apostolic churches had overturned twenty centuries of covenant practice, I would expect a controversy in the text, and the paedobaptist is right that I cannot show him one. I read the silences my way, through Jeremiah and through every narrated baptism. But I hold my conclusion knowing that Calvin and Murray and Ferguson read the same texts with clean hands and came out elsewhere, and that their account of grace speaking over a child before the child can answer is not sentimentality. It is a serious theology of a gracious God, and some of what it guards, the priority of God's promise over my profession, my own tradition is poorer for guarding less well.

On the Supper, I will confess to movement. I was formed in churches where the Supper was a memorial, and quarterly, and brief, and I have come to believe we were right about the grammar and wrong about the weight. Zwingli's exegesis still persuades me. The rock was Christ, I am the vine, this is the Lord's Passover, the Bible speaks in exactly this covenant-meal figure, and do this in remembrance of Me remains the Lord's own stated purpose, which no account of the Supper is permitted to make embarrassing. But 1 Corinthians 10:16 will not let me stop at remembering. Is it not a participation in the blood of Christ, Paul asks, and he expects the answer yes, and a bare symbol does not carry sanctions of sickness and death. So I have been pulled, text by text, toward Calvin, a true feeding on a true Christ, by the Spirit, received through faith, and I notice with some comfort that my own confessional ancestors were already there, the Second London Baptist Confession of 1689 says that worthy receivers spiritually receive and feed upon Christ crucified, which is Geneva's doctrine in Baptist dress. Call my position a memorialism that has read Calvin and repented of the word mere. Where I part from Wittenberg and Rome is at Christology, heaven must receive Him until the time for restoring all things, and I will not bend the true humanity of the ascended Christ to solve a eucharistic problem. But Luther's for you still convicts me, because his deepest instinct was pastoral and it was right, the gift must not rest on the quality of the receiver's faith. I answer him that the promise, not the presence-in-bread, is what bears that weight. I am not certain he would be satisfied, and there are nights I am not either.

And one confession before I close, because self-implication is the house rule and this doctrine has earned it from me. I have served the Supper with my mind on the clock. I have said the words of institution while thinking about the sermon that preceded them, and handed the tray down a row as if it were the offering plate coming back. Whatever the right metaphysics of that Table, no view on this page, not even the lowest, permits what I have sometimes made of it. If the memorialist is right, I was careless with the covenant oath of the church. If Calvin is right, I hurried past a feeding. If Luther or Rome is right, God have mercy. The doctrine of the Supper has many defensible positions. Indifference at the Table is not one of them, and it is the one I have actually practiced most. That, more than any argument above, is what I am trying to reform.
charitableDisagreement:
Begin with the grief, because this doctrine carries a specific one, and it has a date. At Marburg in 1529, Luther and Zwingli agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles, on everything the Reformation had bled for, and broke fellowship over the fifteenth. Witnesses report Luther telling the Swiss they had a different spirit. Within two years Zwingli was dead on a battlefield, and the two halves of Protestantism have communed separately from that day to this. Whatever else Marburg teaches, it teaches that this argument is old, that it was conducted at the highest level by men who both feared God, and that the meal Christ gave to bind His people together has been the visible seam of their division for five centuries. Anyone who enters this debate cheerfully has not understood it.

Now the triage, stated as plainly as I can. First-order, and not on the table for negotiation among Christians: that Christ instituted both signs and commanded His church to keep them until He comes, and that in them, as everywhere in the gospel, grace is God's act before it is our response. A church that discards baptism and the Supper, or empties them into pure ceremony with no command behind them, has left something Christ built. Second-order, and the substance of this whole page: the subjects and mode of baptism, and the manner of Christ's presence in the Supper. These divide faithful churches. They do not divide the faith. A Presbyterian who sprinkles the infant children of believers, a Baptist who immerses professing disciples, a Lutheran who receives the body in and under the bread, and a memorialist who takes the cup as covenant remembrance can each recite the same creed without crossing their fingers, and church history is full of them dying for the same Lord. Third-order, room inside one congregation: frequency, wine or the cup's contents, who serves, common loaf or trays, and most of the questions that actually generate church conflict, which ought to humble us about our sense of proportion.

Hear what each tradition is guarding before you fire at it. The paedobaptist is guarding the priority of grace, God speaking over a child before the child can answer, and the household shape of the covenant promises. The credobaptist is guarding a regenerate church and the integrity of the sign, water that means what it says about faith. The Catholic and the Lutheran are guarding the objectivity of the gift, a Christ who is really there whether or not I feel Him, and the Incarnation's own logic, God giving Himself through creatures. The Reformed believer is guarding the true humanity of the ascended Christ and the Spirit's honor as the one who joins us to Him. The memorialist is guarding the finished, unrepeatable sacrifice and the church from superstition, from adoring the sign in place of the Savior. Not one of those is an unworthy thing to guard. These are five watchmen posted around the same two gifts, each facing the danger the others have their backs to, and most of the polemics of the last five hundred years consist of watchmen shooting each other.

So is it a hill to die on? The signs themselves, yes. Christians have in fact died rather than profane them, and the church must keep them or stop calling herself the church. The mode, the subjects, the metaphysics of presence, no. These are second-order questions, and the evidence for that is not theological softness but the observable fact that faithful, Bible-honoring, Christ-confessing churches have held every position on this page while producing martyrs, missionaries, and saints. Practice your church's conviction with your whole heart, because half-held convictions serve no one. Fence what your conscience requires you to fence, and grieve the fence while you keep it. But be slow, achingly slow, to conclude that the believer at the other table, remembering the same death, proclaiming the same Lord, waiting for the same return, is doing something other than obeying the same command you are. At every one of these tables, in every one of these traditions, the words underneath are identical. Given for you. Until He comes. We argue about the middle of the sentence. We have never disagreed about either end.

relatedDebates.note: The sacraments are ecclesiology enacted. Who may be baptized is finally a question about who belongs to the church, and who may commune is a question about where its boundary runs. The church page takes up the nature, government, and marks of the church directly, and the Reformers counted the right administration of the sacraments among those marks.

relatedDebates.topic: How the whole story fits: covenant frameworks
relatedDebates.note: The baptism debate is largely the covenant debate wearing water. Whether the covenant with Abraham and the new covenant are one covenant of grace in two administrations, or distinct arrangements with distinct membership, quietly decides most of the argument between credo and paedo before a single baptism text is opened. The covenant frameworks page argues that question on its own terms.

relatedDebates.topic: How are we saved, and the means of grace
relatedDebates.note: Every account of the sacraments presupposes an account of how grace reaches a person, through appointed creaturely means, or immediately to faith, or both in concert. The old disputes over ex opere operato, the sacrament working by the work performed, versus reception through faith alone, are the soteriology debate localized to water, bread, and wine.

relatedDebates.topic: Who may come to the Table
relatedDebates.note: Open, close, and closed communion, whether children of the church should commune, whether the Table is fenced by membership, profession, or conscience. These are pastoral questions every congregation answers in practice each time the bread is passed, and most of them are third-order questions handled with first-order feelings, which is why they need naming.
